summary:
Siembra Inteligente is a mobile app that helps smallholder farmers in Peru's Chira valley (Piura) decide what to plant, when, and how to rotate crops as the climate shifts. A farmer marks their plot on a map, matches their soil to one of three types, and chooses a priority: less climate risk, saving water or restoring their soil.

Our open-source backend combines NASA Earth observations (NASA POWER climate, MODIS NDVI vegetation trends, SMAP soil moisture and GPM IMERG rainfall) with SoilGrids soil data and crop parameters. It ranks crop rotations under three climate scenarios: heavy rains, normal and dry. For each option it estimates irrigation water, climate-risk months, a planting calendar and a two-year soil outlook. Two NASA POWER water indicators, local rain and the upstream rain that fills the Poechos reservoir, demote thirsty crops when water looks scarce.

The interface is built for low digital literacy and weak rural signal: simple language, large buttons, and Semi, a guide who introduces every screen and reads it aloud in Spanish.

Piura's farms swing between El Niño floods and droughts, yet smallholders rarely get satellite data that could protect their harvests. Siembra Inteligente turns NASA data into a practical planting decision.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Siembra Inteligente is a mobile app backed by an open-source API. A farmer in the Chira valley (Piura, Peru) marks their plot on a satellite map, says which of three soils theirs looks like (sandy, loamy or clayey), what they planted last and for how many campaigns in a row, and what matters most: less climate risk, saving water or restoring their soil. They can also add restrictions, such as having no buyer for cotton or expecting little water.

The backend answers for three climate scenarios at once (heavy rains, normal and dry), each built from years of observed NASA POWER climate. For every crop rotation it estimates irrigation water per hectare (reference evapotranspiration with Hargreaves-Samani, crop coefficients and effective rain adjusted by soil texture), climate-risk months, a planting calendar and how the soil will end up after two years. It then ranks the rotations for every priority, so the app can re-sort them without a new request.

Other NASA data refine that picture. MODIS NDVI shows whether the plot's greenness is rising or falling, SMAP reports how wet the topsoil has been, and GPM IMERG measures the rain the current campaign actually got. Two water indicators compare the last months of rain and root-zone wetness, and the rain of the upper basin that fills the Poechos reservoir, against the previous ten years. When water looks scarce, water-hungry crops move down the list. The Clima screen adds a 7-day forecast and how the last weeks compare with normal.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Small producers rarely see the satellite data that could protect their harvest. Siembra Inteligente turns it into a decision they can act on: what to plant, when, how much water it will need, and what happens to their soil if they keep repeating the same crop. Our goal is to help farmers in a valley that swings between El Niño floods and droughts choose rotations that use less water and rebuild their soil, before the season starts rather than after the loss.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

Backend: Python 3.11, FastAPI, Pydantic, httpx, pandas, xarray, earthaccess and diskcache, tested with pytest and respx, linted with ruff, run in Docker and deployed on Railway with GitHub Actions CI. Data: NASA POWER, MODIS (ORNL DAAC and AppEEARS), SMAP, GPM IMERG, ISRIC SoilGrids and Open-Meteo.

App: Flutter and Dart for Android, iOS and web, with Riverpod, go_router, flutter_map and on-device text-to-speech. Base map: Sentinel-2 cloudless by EOX. No special hardware: it runs on an ordinary Android phone.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

The farmer's own knowledge counts: the soil they recognize in their hand overrides SoilGrids, which averages 250 m around the plot. With no public data on the reservoir level, we approximate the irrigation water reaching the valley with the rain at the four headwater points that feed it. Every explanation is a plain sentence built from the numbers, and Semi, a guide character, introduces each screen and reads it aloud.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Users with low digital literacy and weak rural signal: large buttons, simple language, voice, large-text and dark-mode support, and the three scenarios returned in a single response so farmers can switch between them offline. If an upstream source fails, the API serves the last real answer for that plot.

Honesty about the data: the indicator rules were fixed before seeing any results. SMAP is reported but not used in the water calculations, because it only measures the top 5 cm. The reservoir indicator says on screen that it is an approximation. NASA POWER cells describe the zone, not the single plot.

Back-testing: we ran both water indicators with data only up to October 2024. Neither flagged the 2025 water shortage, which tells us that rain alone is not enough and that reservoir data is the next step.

Limits: the agronomic parameters are examples, flagged as such by the API, until agronomists validate them. US-only datasets from the resource list were left out because the pilot is in Peru.

AI tools: the team used Anthropic's Claude (Claude Code and Claude chat) for coding and debugging, writing and editing documentation, interpreting the drought back-test, and designing Semi, the guide character, which the app labels as AI-created. The product itself uses no AI: recommendations come from fixed, documented rules applied to NASA data.
